stages.title: The k closest
stages.say: Return the k values in a binary search tree closest to the target, in ascending order.
stages.require: Implement `ClosestBstK.KClosest(root, target, k)`. Ties go to the smaller value. k outside 0..n → `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.

listen: Restates the problem and asks the clarifying questions that change the code (Output order? (Ascending.); Ties in distance? (The smaller value wins.))
States the data structure, the invariant and the complexity before prompting
Reads AI output before running it

1.a: If a value is among the k closest, every value between it and the target is closer, so it is in too.

2.a: Two stacks — predecessors and successors of the target — then merge k steps: O(h + k).

4.q: A huge BST and small k.
4.a: The two-stack version never touches the rest of the tree.

5.a: Find K Closest Elements (658) — the same window idea on an array, with binary search for the start.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: Given a **binary search tree**, a target number and k, return the **k values closest to the target**, in ascending order.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Output order? (Ascending.)
- Ties in distance? (The smaller value wins.)
- Is k ≤ the number of nodes? (Reject anything else.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: An in-order walk lists a BST's values in sorted order, and the k closest values to any target form a **contiguous window** of that sorted list. Start with the whole list and drop whichever end is farther until k remain.

learn.title: 4 · Approach

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- A max-heap of size k over all values — works (O(n log k)) but ignores the BST order.
- Sorting by distance and taking k — then re-sorting by value.
- Getting the tie rule backwards when trimming the ends.
